description:
Section C — Untrusted Input at Protocol Boundaries; Section F — Logging Output Safety.

parse_base_url at crate-jmap-base-client/src/client.rs:741-774 rejects empty input, non-http/https schemes, path components, query strings, and fragments. It does NOT reject URLs that carry credentials in the authority component (the RFC 3986 `userinfo` field — `https://user:password@host/`). url::Url::parse accepts this form and stores password() and username().

When such a URL is passed through to reqwest and a request later fails, reqwest's Error carries a reqwest::Url that retains the user-info component. HttpError::url() at error.rs:80-82 returns it via to_string() — and url::Url::Display includes the user-info component verbatim (RFC 3986 §7.5 explicitly warns against this; url crate Display follows the lossless-round-trip rule, not the safe-display rule). HttpError::Display delegates to the inner reqwest::Error which itself includes the URL in many failure messages.

# What goes wrong (confidentiality)

A caller that accidentally passes `https://alice:secret@jmap.example.com` as base_url (or one that interpolates user input into the base_url string) sees the password in:

- ClientError::Http(HttpError) error message when any request fails
- Any tracing::*-style log that captures the error
- Any stderr / panic / Debug-format of the HttpError
- The url() accessor's owned String return

The existing JMAP-6r7c.35 finding flags Session.username PII; this is the analogous defect at the URL layer for actual credentials (password component of the authority).

# Suggested fix

In parse_base_url, after url::Url::parse succeeds, reject the URL if parsed.username() is non-empty or parsed.password() is Some. Emit ClientError::InvalidArgument with a message that does NOT echo the URL back (to avoid the error chain itself leaking the credential the caller just tried to supply). Suggested text: `'base_url must not contain user-info; pass credentials via AuthProvider instead'`.

Defense in depth: HttpError::url() could also strip user-info before returning the String. RFC 3986 §7.5 is the canonical guidance.

# What this is NOT

This is NOT a vulnerability of the JMAP protocol itself. JMAP authenticates via the Authorization header, not URL user-info. The defect is that the BASE client accepts a URL shape that ferries credentials into log output without the caller noticing.

# Probe (read-only)

Verify by writing a one-line probe:

```rust
let u = url::Url::parse("https://alice:secret@jmap.example.com/").unwrap();
println!("{}", u);  // outputs: https://alice:secret@jmap.example.com/
println!("{:?}", u.password());  // Some("secret")
```

(Do not run from this review session; included as the probe a /do-beads session can run.)

# References

- RFC 3986 §3.2.1, §7.5 — user-info syntax + security implications
- url crate docs: Url::password, Url::username, Url::Display behavior
title: parse_base_url accepts user-info in URL authority; credentials leak via HttpError Display
